prepared_answers_en.tell_me_about_yourself: I studied two degrees at Universidad de los Andes, Systems and Computer Engineering and Chemical Engineering, and I graduated in 2025. Then I did a ten-month internship at AWS. I built internal campaign web applications with KPI tracking and team dashboards. More than two hundred sales professionals across Latin America used them during each four-week campaign. As my own practice project, I also built a multi-agent AI prototype on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. And with a team of just two interns, we won the AWS LATAM New Hire Jam Day hackathon. We were the only LATAM team to finish all fourteen challenges. Since April I've been a Junior Cloud Support Engineer at Amadeus, working with Kubernetes and OpenShift. I wrote a small read-only Python tool that summarizes our monitoring before I review it. Now I want to build software full time, on a product people really depend on. And this role is built for early-career engineers who like hard problems.
prepared_answers_en.why_docplanner: First, impact: Docplanner helps millions of patients find a doctor and book an appointment, in Spain and in Latin America, where I'm from. Second, your culture: AI-assisted development is your default. And third, healthcare and AI together. With chemical engineering and a machine learning thesis on proteins, that's where I want to grow.
prepared_answers_en.why_this_role: It's built for early-career engineers who like hard problems and coding, and that's my profile. I already work with part of your stack. I use TypeScript and React in my portfolio site, and NestJS in my coursework. At Amadeus I use Kubernetes, OpenShift, Grafana and Prometheus every day. And it's my step from supporting systems to building them.
prepared_answers_en.challenge_overcome: Situation: at the AWS LATAM New Hire Jam Day 2025 there were 14 technical challenges, and my team was just two interns, one person fewer than the other teams. Task: I took one of the hardest ones, connecting two virtual machines through a secure, authenticated tunnel. Action: my deployment kept failing. Instead of skipping it, I re-read the whole specification and found a key requirement at the very bottom that showed my environment had been misconfigured from the start. I redeployed it once, cleanly, validating each step, and after about three hours it worked. Result: no other team completed that challenge, and we became the only LATAM team to finish all 14, so we won. What I learned: read the spec fully, question your own setup, and rebuild cleanly instead of guessing.
prepared_answers_en.initiative: At AWS, the sales team needed landing pages for their campaigns. The plan was to buy them from an external vendor, for about two thousand dollars per campaign. I raised my hand and said I could build them internally, and save that money. At first, they weren't sure an intern could do it. So I built the first one in about four days, within Amazon's internal rules and approved services. I also found a supported way to use my own HTML and CSS. It worked, and after that, I built all the campaign pages. More than two hundred sales professionals across Latin America used them during each four-week campaign. What I took from it is that if I can see a better way, I'd rather offer it and prove it than just accept the default.
prepared_answers_en.impact: A good example is the campaign landing pages I built at AWS. The plan was to buy them from an external vendor for about two thousand dollars per campaign. I offered to build them internally instead. At first they weren't sure an intern could do it, so I built the first one, within Amazon's internal rules and approved services. I gathered feedback from teams in several countries, including Brazil, and found a supported way to use my own HTML and CSS so the pages were clear for busy sales teams. The impact: we didn't need the vendor, I ended up building all the campaign pages, and more than two hundred sales professionals across Latin America used them during each four-week campaign.
prepared_answers_en.collaboration: Situation: at Amadeus I work in a 24/7 Follow-the-Sun team supporting high-availability travel platforms. Task: incidents have to move quickly between people, shifts and engineering teams. Action: I escalate early and with clear written evidence, so the engineering team can act right away, and I document procedures in runbooks so the next person on shift doesn't start from zero. Result: the operation as a whole resolves over 90% of around 4,600 weekly incidents at the frontline, and clear handoffs are a big part of that. At AWS I also turned feedback from stakeholders in several countries into features for the campaign apps.
prepared_answers_en.feedback: Situation: as a teaching assistant for Programming in Python at Universidad de los Andes, I was helping a student who was stuck on an exercise. Task: figure out why she was stuck and help her move forward. Action: I started by checking the programming concepts the exercise needed, one by one, and she knew all of them. She clearly knew how to program. So I kept asking questions until I found the real blocker: the exercise needed some fairly advanced math, and she didn't understand the problem itself. I told her directly that her programming was solid and what was blocking her was the problem statement. And I suggested that if it ever happened in an exam, she shouldn't panic: it's a programming exam, not a math exam, so she should ask to clarify the problem without fear instead of letting it limit her. Result: she could see that her programming wasn't the problem, and that asking to understand the problem was the way through. What I took from it: good feedback starts with finding the real blocker, not the obvious one. It's the same thing I do now: understand the problem fully before trying to solve it.
prepared_answers_en.conflict_disagreement: In a chemical engineering lab project, I joined a group that already knew each other, and they didn't really trust me yet. We had to make cheese, and I was in charge of the milk. They told me to buy a regular long-life whole milk. I researched it and found that long-life milk is heated so much that its proteins change. So it won't curdle properly for cheese. I explained this, but they didn't believe me. So instead of arguing, I bought both milks. In the lab they tried theirs first. After three hours, it still hadn't curdled. So we switched to mine, and we lost three hours, not another lab day. That was the first time the group really listened to me. What I took from it: when I disagree, I bring evidence and a backup plan. And next time, I'd share the source earlier.
prepared_answers_en.strength: Problem solving with persistence. If something is possible, I assume there's a way, and I like being the one who finds it. The hackathon is the clearest example: I didn't skip the hardest challenge, I went back to the specification, found what was wrong in my own setup and rebuilt it cleanly. Outside work I practise on LeetCode and enjoy puzzles and escape rooms.
prepared_answers_en.weakness: I don't have much experience with large production codebases yet. I compensate by reading documentation deeply and asking early, with clear evidence of what I've tried. I used to keep debugging alone for too long; the hackathon taught me to step back and re-read the spec, and Amadeus taught me to escalate early.
prepared_answers_en.salary_expectations:
As I mentioned in my application, I'm looking at forty to forty-eight thousand euros gross a year, depending on the full package. What does the package include, like bonus or benefits?
(If they already described the package, drop the question. If they say their band is lower, use 'salary_below_band'.)
prepared_answers_en.other_processes: Yes, a few, at different stages, which is normal at this point. But this one is a top priority for me. If timelines become an issue, I'll let you know openly.
prepared_answers_en.day_to_day_amadeus: I'm part of a 24/7 Follow-the-Sun support team for high-availability travel platforms. I troubleshoot deployed microservices on Linux and Kubernetes/OpenShift, for example by recycling pods. I run health and performance checks with Grafana and Prometheus, and when an issue needs the engineering team, I escalate it with clear written evidence. I also document procedures in runbooks. It's a big operation: the team handles around 4,600 incidents a week and resolves over 90% at the frontline.
prepared_answers_en.what_did_you_build_at_aws: At work, I built internal campaign web applications with KPI tracking, prize management and team dashboards. They went live and were used by more than 200 sales professionals across Latin America during each four-week campaign. I gathered requirements from stakeholders in several countries, including Brazil, and designed within Amazon's internal rules and approved services. And on my own, two side projects. First, a personal tool with Amazon Q Developer CLI that generates creative HTML emails formatted for Outlook, to work more efficiently. Second, as my practice project for an internal AWS Solutions Architect program, a multi-agent prototype written in Python with the AWS CDK, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Strands Agents: an orchestrator coordinating specialized agents, with tool calling, memory and RAG over a knowledge base.
prepared_answers_en.chemical_engineering_fit: I actually started in Chemical Engineering. Then I took programming, and I liked it so much that I decided to study both, in parallel. What I liked was the idea of understanding chemistry with the logic of computing. Proteins are the clearest example for me. A protein is a sequence of amino acids, written by the genetic code, and to me it's like code we're still learning to read. I like knowing that everything has a pattern, and finding patterns is exactly what software is good at. My thesis brought both together: I used machine learning to predict how stable proteins are with heat. So for me the two degrees aren't separate: software is how I understand science. And that's part of why a healthcare product like Docplanner interests me.
prepared_answers_en.freelance_payments: As a freelancer I built a Power Automate and Power Apps workflow that calls a Colombian bank's existing REST API, for a client company that needed to pay out more than 2,000 transfers a week. I didn't build the API; I consumed it from a low-code flow, kept the credentials in Azure Key Vault, and added dashboards so the client could see successful and reversed transactions.
prepared_answers_en.stack_node:
I haven't used Node.js in production yet. In my full-stack coursework, I built back ends with NestJS, which runs on Node. I wrote them in TypeScript and tested them with Jest. My portfolio site is Next.js, React and TypeScript. So my gap is Node in production, and I close gaps like that by building.
(Never cut the last sentence.)
prepared_answers_en.relocation: I live in Bogotá right now. I'm a Spanish citizen, so I don't need a visa or a work permit. I'd move to Spain for this role. Since it's remote, I'm flexible on the city. I'm leaning towards Valencia, but Barcelona would also work for me. My notice period is two weeks, and I'd plan the move so I'm already living in Spain on my start date.
prepared_answers_en.why_leaving_amadeus:
I've learned a lot at Amadeus about production. But after six months, the work has become repetitive, to the point that I automated part of it. I want more depth, and above all, I want to build software, not only support it. And I'm a Spanish citizen, and I'd like to live and work in Spain.
(If the script was already mentioned, say "as I mentioned" instead of describing it. Spanish: "He aprendido mucho en Amadeus sobre sistemas en producción. Pero después de seis meses, el trabajo se volvió repetitivo, tanto que automaticé parte de él. Quiero más profundidad y, sobre todo, construir software, no solo darle soporte. Y soy ciudadana española, y quiero vivir y trabajar en España.")
prepared_answers_en.little_experience: That's true, and this role is designed for early-career engineers. What I can show is the hackathon win, internal campaign apps used by more than two hundred sales professionals during each four-week campaign, three AWS certifications, and real production operations experience at Amadeus.
prepared_answers_en.ai_tools: I'm not tied to one tool. AI helps me work more efficiently, but my work is based on understanding the problem. I use AI search a lot, to find solutions faster instead of spending half an hour searching. At AWS, I also used Amazon Q Developer CLI to build my own small tool for HTML emails. And I always read, test and review what it gives me.
prepared_answers_en.mistake_or_failure: A real failure for me was my first thesis attempt, in chemical engineering. I chose the topic I loved most, proteins, and I spent days in the lab running experiments. I based my method on my director's recommendations, because I trusted them completely. In the end, the thesis didn't pass. And what I own is this: I relied on a single source. I didn't research enough on my own, and I didn't ask other people to check the approach. So for my final thesis, I worked with two directors, and it passed. What I learned is to validate an approach with more than one source.
prepared_answers_en.thesis_if_asked: If they ask about the thesis: I used ESM-2, a language model trained on protein sequences, so it reads proteins almost like text. I applied it to more than twenty thousand proteins and trained PyTorch models to predict how stable each one is with heat. The best one, an LSTM, reached an R squared of 0.74, with an average error of about four and a half degrees. I served it as a web app with Docker.
prepared_answers_en.multi_agent_explained_simply: Happy to explain it simply. Think of it as a small team of AI agents working together, instead of one person, or one agent, doing everything. The scenario I chose was a gym that wanted an AI personal trainer. So there was an orchestrator agent that split up the work, and two specialized agents: one for nutrition and one for training. They used tool calling, so the agents could actually take actions, not just answer questions. They also had memory, and they could search a knowledge base to find relevant information before responding. All of that depending on each agent's specific task. My part was all of it: I built it alone, as my practice project for an internal AWS Solutions Architect program. I wrote it in Python with the AWS CDK, running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Strands Agents. It was a prototype, so the goal was to understand how this kind of multi-agent system can work for real tasks, not to ship a finished product.
prepared_answers_en.multi_agent_who_for: It wasn't for a team or a client. It was my own practice project, and I built it alone, from start to finish. During the internship I was preparing to become a Solutions Architect at AWS. That path has three internal certifications, in a program called AWSome Builder, and each one is based on a project. I passed the first two before I joined Amadeus. You choose a customer scenario yourself, you build it, and you present it as if you were talking to a customer. My scenario was a gym that wanted an AI personal trainer for its members: an orchestrator agent, a nutrition agent and a training agent. The point is to practise three things. First, explaining technical ideas in a simple way. Second, exploring different AWS services and handling the questions a customer would ask. And third, showing the final cost, in a way that doesn't scare the customer.
prepared_answers_en.why_not_stay_at_aws:
I was preparing for a Solutions Architect role. But I saw it's mostly customer calls on one specialty, and I prefer building. So I got closer to the Professional Services junior team, and in January it was closed in the layoffs. AWS offered me another internship, but no full-time role. So I joined Amadeus to learn production up close.
(Only if asked about the program: I passed two of the three internal AWSome Builder certifications. Only if asked which team: it was the team I did the hackathon with.)
prepared_answers_en.schedule_now:
Right now I'm on a 24/7 Follow-the-Sun team, so my schedule isn't a fixed Monday to Friday. Some weeks that includes weekend shifts. That's normal in production support, and I understand why it exists. I don't mind working a weekend when it's needed, as long as it's planned and compensated. But as a regular schedule, I prefer Monday to Friday, because weekends are my time for family, friends, rest and learning.
Only if they ask directly whether the weekend work is compensated: "It isn't compensated separately right now. That's why, for a future role, I'd want weekend work to be planned and compensated."
If they ask about on-call at Docplanner: "I'm open to occasional on-call, as long as it's planned and compensated."
prepared_answers_en.proudest_experience:
The experience I'm proudest of is winning the AWS LATAM New Hire Jam Day hackathon in 2025. There were fourteen technical challenges, and my team was just two interns, one person fewer than the other teams. I took one of the hardest ones: connecting two virtual machines through a secure, authenticated tunnel. My deployment kept failing, so instead of skipping it, I re-read the whole specification and found a requirement at the very bottom I had missed. I redeployed once, cleanly, and after about three hours it worked. No other team completed that challenge, and we were the only LATAM team to finish all fourteen. Why I'm proud of it: I was an intern in the sales organization, and I wasn't sure I belonged among engineers. That day showed me I can solve hard technical problems if I keep going and question my own setup.
(If the hackathon was already told earlier in this call, don't retell it. Say: "It's the hackathon I mentioned." Then only the why: I was an intern in the sales organization, and I wasn't sure I belonged among engineers. That day showed me I can solve hard technical problems if I keep going and question my own setup.)
prepared_answers_en.initiative_amadeus_script: Situation: at Amadeus, part of my work is health checks and incident analysis across several monitoring dashboards. Task: nobody asked me to change that, but I knew it could be done better. Action: I wrote a small Python script that uses my own authenticated access, read-only, to query the same data the monitoring pages show. It pulls the key graphs and incidents and gives me a summary with links to the relevant graphs and a short explanation. Result: my analysis now starts from the most relevant information, so I find problems faster, including the harder ones. It's still a personal tool; my next step is to polish it so I can propose it to the team.

prepared_answers_en.received_feedback:
The hardest feedback I got was on my first thesis attempt, in chemical engineering. I chose the topic I loved most, proteins, and I spent days in the lab running experiments. I based my method on my director's recommendations, because I trusted them completely. In the end, the feedback was clear: the thesis wasn't good enough to pass. That was hard to hear. So I looked at what I could change myself, and it was how I validate my work. I had relied on a single source. For my final thesis, I chose machine learning on proteins, which combined both of my degrees. I worked with two directors and checked my approach with more than one source. That thesis passed. What I learned is to validate an approach with more than one source, early.
(If the thesis was already told in this call: "Going back to the thesis I mentioned, the feedback was clear: it wasn't good enough to pass. So I looked at what I could change myself, which was how I validate my work. For my final thesis, I chose machine learning on proteins, worked with two directors and checked my approach with more than one source. That one passed. What I learned is to validate early, with more than one source.")

I check the dashboards for each application and connection, one by one, to see if it's an application problem, a network problem or something else. I also look for recent changes linked to it. If it needs the engineering team, I escalate with clear written evidence of what I've checked. Because those steps repeat every time, I automated part of them with my own read-only script.

So I always reviewed every email and fixed the output before using it. That's why I never trust AI output without reading and testing it.

prepared_answers_en.code_bug: It was a university project in object-oriented design. My code kept failing, and I couldn't find why. I commented code out and debugged step by step, but everything looked right. In the end, after about an hour with my professor, we found it. There were two classes with almost the same name, like Book and Books. The editor had created the second one automatically, with a quick create-class fix, and I hadn't noticed. What I took from it: always check what a tool generated for me. It's the same reason I review everything AI generates today.
